concepts.name: Resistance and muscle adaptation
concepts.summary: Explain that muscles adapt to challenging loads by getting stronger and larger over time, with the nervous system driving early strength gains.

concepts.name: Core compound lifts
concepts.summary: Name the main compound movements such as squat, deadlift, bench press, overhead press and row, and the muscles each trains.

concepts.name: Sets, reps and load
concepts.summary: Define a repetition, a set, the load lifted and rest between sets, and read a basic workout written in those terms.

concepts.name: Neutral spine and bracing
concepts.summary: Explain why keeping a neutral spine and bracing the trunk protects the back and transfers force during lifts.

concepts.name: Warm-up routine
concepts.summary: Describe why a general warm-up and lighter ramp-up sets prepare the body before heavy work.

concepts.name: Gym safety essentials
concepts.summary: Understand how to use spotters, safety bars, collars and sensible loading to lift without injury.

concepts.name: Rest and sleep basics
concepts.summary: Understand that muscles recover and grow between sessions through rest, sleep and adequate food, not during the workout itself.

misconceptions.text: Lifting weights makes you bulky quickly, especially for women.
Muscle grows during the workout itself rather than during recovery afterwards.
Lifting with a rounded back is fine as long as the weight feels manageable.

concepts.name: Technique for each core lift
concepts.summary: Perform the squat, hip hinge, press and row with correct bar path, joint positions and depth using light to moderate loads.

concepts.name: Progressive overload
concepts.summary: Apply small, regular increases in weight, reps or sets so that training stays challenging as the body adapts.

concepts.name: Rep ranges and goals
concepts.summary: Explain how lower rep ranges favour maximal strength while moderate ranges suit muscle size, and choose a range for a goal.

concepts.name: Effort and proximity to failure
concepts.summary: Use reps in reserve or perceived exertion to judge how hard a set is and stop short of form breakdown.

concepts.name: Basic weekly split
concepts.summary: Arrange a simple full-body or upper/lower weekly schedule that trains each muscle group about twice a week.

concepts.name: Training log keeping
concepts.summary: Record exercises, loads, reps and effort each session and use the record to choose the next workout.

concepts.name: Protein and energy intake
concepts.summary: Explain that adequate protein and enough total calories support muscle gain and recovery.

misconceptions.text: Adding weight every session is the only way to progress, regardless of form.
Light weights for high reps will tone muscle while heavy weights only build bulk.
Every set must go to complete failure to be effective.

concepts.name: Weekly volume management
concepts.summary: Plan and adjust the number of hard sets per muscle group each week to fall between productive minimum and recoverable maximum.

concepts.name: Exercise selection and balance
concepts.summary: Choose main lifts and accessories that cover all movement patterns and balance pushing, pulling and leg work for a given goal.

concepts.name: Periodised programme structure
concepts.summary: Organise training into blocks with planned changes in volume and intensity, including a scheduled easier week.

concepts.name: Plateau diagnosis
concepts.summary: Analyse a stall by examining recovery, nutrition, volume, technique and programming to find the likely cause.

concepts.name: Fatigue and deloads
concepts.summary: Recognise accumulated fatigue from performance, sleep and joint signs and decide when to reduce load or volume.

concepts.name: Injury versus soreness
concepts.summary: Distinguish normal muscle soreness from pain signalling injury and adapt exercises to train around a problem.

concepts.name: Range of motion and tempo
concepts.summary: Control tempo and use full, controlled ranges of motion to deliver tension to the target muscle.

misconceptions.text: More volume is always better, so adding sets endlessly speeds up growth.
Muscle soreness is a reliable measure of how effective a workout was.
Changing exercises every session keeps muscles guessing and is needed for progress.

concepts.name: Autoregulated load selection
concepts.summary: Adjust daily loads and sets from readiness and effort ratings instead of fixed percentages alone.

concepts.name: Individualising programme variables
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a lifter's training age, recovery capacity, schedule and response should shape frequency, volume and intensity.

concepts.name: Biomechanics and leverages
concepts.summary: Analyse how body proportions affect lift mechanics and adjust stance, grip and bar position to suit them.

concepts.name: Periodisation model comparison
concepts.summary: Compare linear, undulating and block models and judge which suits a given goal, level and timeline.

concepts.name: Specificity and peaking
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to bias training toward specific lifts and taper fatigue to express maximal strength on a target date.

concepts.name: Weak point analysis
concepts.summary: Identify the phase or muscle limiting a lift and select targeted variations or accessories to address it.

concepts.name: Evidence quality appraisal
concepts.summary: Judge fitness claims and studies by sample, design and practical relevance before changing a programme.

misconceptions.text: There is one optimal programme or technique that works identically for every lifter.
Autoregulation means training only when you feel like it and skipping hard work.
Findings from studies on untrained participants apply directly to advanced lifters.

concepts.name: Designing multi-year training plans
concepts.summary: Create long-range plans that sequence phases of building, specialisation and maintenance across years and changing life circumstances.

concepts.name: Fatigue management models
concepts.summary: Evaluate fatigue models and their limits to optimise the stimulus relative to recovery cost.

concepts.name: Coaching and technique correction
concepts.summary: Design cueing and progression strategies that diagnose and fix faults for lifters of differing abilities.

concepts.name: Custom programme design for populations
concepts.summary: Create safe, effective programmes for older adults, rehabilitating lifters, or those with limited equipment or time.

concepts.name: Critique of training systems
concepts.summary: Evaluate popular training systems against principles and evidence to find their strengths, weaknesses and appropriate users.

concepts.name: Integrating nutrition and recovery
concepts.summary: Synthesise training with energy balance phases, sleep and stress management to meet strength and physique targets.

concepts.name: Data-driven programme refinement
concepts.summary: Judge training data trends to decide when to change a plan, separating noise from true progress.

misconceptions.text: Advanced lifters should simply do the same methods as beginners with heavier weights.
A popular programme that worked for a champion will work for any client.
Every dip in performance means the programme has failed and must be changed.
